attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the firm 'will', the cascade triggered by a first token-budget cut, and the lack of any deadline. The wording is hyperbolic but not hedged, so it counts as a scoreable forecast.

contract.note: The plain reading is that one visible budget cut triggers others to follow. That is fair and ordinary. Requiring proof of imitation follows from 'send the rest of them'. The contract rightly says that with no deadline, the absence of a cascade cannot contradict the claim.

evidence.note: Accenture's cut in central Claude allowances took effect 1 Oct 2026. This bears on the antecedent only. It shows no cascade of other companies following, so it is not evidence of the outcome.
Microsoft restricted staff AI use in August 2026, before the Accenture cut. Nothing attributes this to copying another company, so it does not show the predicted imitative rush.
Accenture's own disclosure presents cost controls as a way to scale AI further. It argues against reading the cuts as an exit, but it cannot settle an undated forecast.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The packet shows several separate cost controls (Microsoft, Accenture) but no documented cascade of companies copying an initiating cut. The early-resolution rule for support is not met, and with an open horizon, no cascade so far is not a failure. The evidence by the cutoff does not settle it.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, stated as fact in his post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the core 70% share and the $54B total. It drops the $28B-in-the-last-month and conditional-$50B details, but the contract restores them as explicit elements. It is a factual observation.

contract.note: The denominator (all operational compute rather than AI compute) is an evaluator choice the speaker did not supply. It is flagged as ambiguous. Reading 'fed' as funding actually paid is reasonable. Because the evidence is missing under any reading, the choice does not change the result here.

evidence.note: Amazon put $5B into Anthropic on 20 Apr 2026, with up to $20B more later. This is consistent with parts of the last-month and conditional amounts, but it is not a complete funding ledger.
Google put $10B in on 24 Apr 2026, with $30B contingent on milestones. Combined with Amazon's $20B, this matches the conditional $50B, but it does not reconcile the $54B or $28B totals.
Microsoft's 'up to $5B' is a commitment ceiling announced Nov 2025. It shows no disbursement amounts or dates.

Epoch estimates OpenAI and Anthropic held 15–20% of the world's AI compute at end-2025. The denominator and period differ from the three-company claim, so it cannot directly contradict the 70% figure.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet records the share of Microsoft, Google and Amazon compute allocated to the two labs, so the 70% claim cannot be checked. Announcements match the conditional $50B, but no ledger reconciles the $54B paid or the $28B in the last month. The Epoch estimate uses a different denominator. The evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps 'sometimes' and both financial clauses. The quality clauses ('mediocre', 'vigilant eye') are rhetorical and cannot be measured; only the financial part is testable.

contract.note: The contract tests offering-level losses on both consumer and enterprise products. That is a plausible reading, since 'a subsidized product that loses Anthropic money' is about one offering. But the enterprise clause could mean consolidated losses, and under that weaker reading the S-1 would support the claim. The contract flags this ambiguity.

evidence.note: Audited 2025 S-1 shows a consolidated net loss, much of it from instrument revaluation, and reports a single segment. It gives no separate consumer and enterprise profit figures, so it cannot test offering-level losses.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's offering-level reading, there are no separate consumer and enterprise profit-and-loss records for 2025. The S-1 reports only one segment and a consolidated loss. That consolidated loss fits the weaker reading but does not meet the support condition. The quality clauses are not measurable. Unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'These numbers' covers the revenue figures just cited as well as capex. The proposition narrows this to capex figures only. The contract restores the revenue-versus-capex scope, so the scoring is not affected.

contract.note: The ordinary reading is that the revenue and capex figures leave out recurring running costs, and treating cost of revenue as running costs is an everyday reading. Both are fair. Using Microsoft FY2025 matches the comparison he had just made.

evidence.note: Microsoft's FY2025 10-K (a third-party hosted copy) reports revenue, cost of revenue, operating expenses and capital additions separately. It also says cost of revenue grew because of cloud growth. So revenue and capex figures leave out running costs.
The Q4 FY2025 earnings call describes capex as long-lived assets, servers and finance leases. That fits the distinction between capex and running costs, but it covers one quarter only.

reviews.rationale: Microsoft's audited FY2025 filing reports revenue and capital additions separately from cost of revenue and operating expenses. The earnings call describes capex as asset purchases. So the revenue and capex figures in the comparison leave out recurring datacenter running costs, as the speaker said. The contract's support condition is met.
